seerah.title: Seerah Timeline
seerah.subtitle: The Life of the Prophet ﷺ

milestones.title: Birth in the Year of the Elephant
milestones.short: Born in Makkah — his father had already passed away.
milestones.body:
In the year 570 CE, in the city of Makkah, a child was born who would one day change the course of human history. That same year, an army from Yemen led by Abraha had marched on Makkah with a great elephant, intending to destroy the Kaaba — but Allah sent flocks of birds carrying stones of baked clay and the army was scattered. The Quraysh called that year the Year of the Elephant, and it was in that year that Muhammad ﷺ was born.

His father, Abdullah ibn Abdul-Muttalib, had passed away before his birth, on a return journey from Yathrib. So the child was born into the care of his mother, Aminah bint Wahb, and his grandfather, Abdul-Muttalib, chief of the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh.

Abdul-Muttalib took the infant in his arms, carried him into the Kaaba, and prayed to Allah, thanking Him for this gift. He named the boy Muhammad — a name uncommon among the Arabs, meaning 'the one who is praised.' Little did the world know then just how thoroughly that name would be honoured.
milestones.takeaway: Every great journey begins with a single birth — and the world rarely knows what it holds until time reveals it.

milestones.title: Life Among Banu Sa'd
milestones.short: The desert years with his wet nurse Halimah.
milestones.body:
As was the custom of noble Makkan families, the infant was given to a wet nurse from the desert — so that he might grow up in the pure desert air, learn the purest Arabic, and be raised strong and free from the constraints of the city.

He was taken by Halimah as-Sa'diyyah of the Banu Sa'd tribe. Barakah — blessing — came into Halimah's household the day she took him in. Her goats gave milk when others did not. Her land grew greener. Her family flourished. Even in his infancy, he carried something the world could not yet name.
milestones.takeaway: Allah places His blessings in the smallest and the youngest — the world simply needs the eyes to see them.

milestones.title: The Mother's Passing
milestones.short: Aminah dies at Al-Abwa; the orphan is six years old.
milestones.body:
When Muhammad ﷺ was six years old, his mother Aminah took him on a journey to Yathrib to visit the grave of his father and to see her relatives from the Banu Najjar. It was a long journey for a small boy, and it was to be their last together.

On the return journey, at a place called Al-Abwa — halfway between Makkah and Madinah — Aminah fell gravely ill. She passed away there, and was buried in that quiet place beneath the desert sun.

The boy returned to Makkah, now fully orphaned — no father, no mother. He was taken in by his grandfather Abdul-Muttalib, who loved him deeply and kept him close, always.
milestones.takeaway: Loss is the teacher of compassion — the orphan who loses his mother becomes, in time, a mercy to all mothers.

milestones.title: The Grandfather's Passing
milestones.short: Abdul-Muttalib dies; the boy passes to his uncle Abu Talib.
milestones.body:
Two years passed. Muhammad ﷺ was now eight years old, and his grandfather Abdul-Muttalib — the respected chief of Banu Hashim — fell ill. On his deathbed, he called his son Abu Talib and entrusted the boy to him.

Abu Talib was a merchant of modest means, but he was respected among the Quraysh, and he accepted the trust without hesitation. He raised Muhammad ﷺ as one of his own children — indeed, some say he loved him more than his own sons.

For the next four decades, until Abu Talib's own death, he remained the Prophet's ﷺ closest protector — through every trial of the Makkan years, through every threat from the Quraysh, Abu Talib stood as an unbreakable wall between his nephew and harm.
milestones.takeaway: A single act of protection can shield a life that will one day shield the world.

milestones.title: First Journey to Syria
milestones.short: The monk Bahira recognises the signs of prophethood.
milestones.body:
At the age of twelve, Muhammad ﷺ accompanied his uncle Abu Talib on a trading journey north to Syria — the land of Bilad ash-Sham. It was his first journey beyond Arabia, and it would leave a lasting impression.

When the caravan stopped at a place called Busra, a Christian monk named Bahira — a man learned in the scriptures of old — noticed something unusual. He had watched caravans pass for years, but this one carried a subtle difference. A cloud seemed to shade one of the travellers. When the group sat beneath a tree, the tree's branches seemed to lean toward the boy.

Bahira invited the caravan to a meal and questioned the boy and his uncle. He examined the boy's eyes, his shoulders, the mark between his shoulder blades. Then he turned to Abu Talib and said: 'Take your nephew back to his homeland and guard him carefully. If the Jews or the Romans learn of him, they will harm him. This boy has a great destiny.'

Abu Talib returned to Makkah sooner than planned, keeping the boy close.
milestones.takeaway: Some signs are only visible to eyes prepared to see them — the world recognises a treasure before it knows its name.

milestones.title: Hilf al-Fudul
milestones.short: The league of the virtuous — defending the oppressed.
milestones.body:
Muhammad ﷺ was now in his early twenties — known across Makkah as Al-Amin, the trustworthy, for his honesty, fairness, and gentle manner. But the city was not always just.

One day, a Yemeni merchant came to Makkah and sold his goods to a powerful Makkan, who then refused to pay. The merchant cried out in the valley of Makkah, appealing to the Quraysh for justice — but no one answered.

In response, a pact was formed between several of the noble clans — the Banu Hashim, the Banu Muttalib, the Banu Zuhrah and others. They called it Hilf al-Fudul — the League of the Virtuous. Its pledge was simple: to defend anyone wronged in Makkah, regardless of tribe or status, so that no one would be oppressed again.

Muhammad ﷺ joined the pact wholeheartedly. And years later, after the coming of Islam, he would still speak of it with affection: 'Had this pact been made in Islam, I would have answered its call.'
milestones.takeaway: Justice is not owned by any one people — anyone who defends the wronged belongs to the family of the righteous.

milestones.title: Marriage to Khadijah
milestones.short: The Prophet ﷺ marries Khadijah at age 25.
milestones.body:
Khadijah bint Khuwaylid was a wealthy and respected merchant of Makkah — a widow who managed a flourishing trade across the region. She had heard of Muhammad ﷺ' honesty and reliability, and she employed him to take her goods to Syria.

He returned with a profit beyond what any of her other agents had brought, and — more importantly — with a character that impressed everyone who dealt with him. When Khadijah's companion Nafisah hinted to him about marriage, he was ready. The two were married, and a partnership began that would shape the world.

The Prophet ﷺ was twenty-five; Khadijah was around forty. For twenty-five years, until her passing, she remained his closest companion, his most trusted advisor, and — when the revelation came — the very first believer in his message. He loved her deeply, and never took another wife during her lifetime.
milestones.takeaway: The greatest missions are sustained by the quietest partnerships — behind every prophet stands a faithful heart.

milestones.title: Rebuilding the Kaaba
milestones.short: His arbitration over the Black Stone.
milestones.body:
By the age of thirty-five, the Prophet ﷺ was known far and wide as Al-Amin — the trustworthy. When a flood damaged the Kaaba and the Quraysh decided to rebuild it, they had no idea that the great test of their city was about to fall into the hands of one man.

The rebuilding went smoothly until the time came to place the Black Stone — Hajar al-Aswad — in its corner. Every clan wanted the honour. Swords were nearly drawn; the Quraysh stood at the edge of a war.

Then an elder suggested: 'Let the first man to enter the gate of the Kaaba decide.' The first to enter was Muhammad ﷺ. The people sighed with relief: 'It is Al-Amin. We accept him.'

He did not choose between the clans. Instead, he spread a cloth on the ground, placed the Black Stone upon it, and asked a chief from each clan to take a corner. Together they raised it into place — with his hands guiding the stone home. In a single act, he turned a quarrel into a shared honour.
milestones.takeaway: Wisdom does not take sides — it finds the solution that lets everyone lift together.

milestones.title: The First Revelation
milestones.short: Jibril comes to the cave of Hira — the Quran begins.
milestones.body:
By the age of forty, Muhammad ﷺ had long withdrawn from the noise of Makkah. He would retreat to a small cave called Hira, high on the rocky mountain of Jabal an-Nur — a bare, silent place overlooking the valley. There he would sit alone for days, reflecting on the world, on its injustices, on the idols his people worshipped, on the One God his ancestor Ibrahim (a.s) had called to.

It was in the month of Ramadan, in the year 610 CE, that something happened that would split human history into before and after.

A presence appeared before him — the angel Jibril (a.s) — and said: Iqra' — Read. The Prophet ﷺ answered, trembling: 'I cannot read.' The angel embraced him tightly, then released him and said again: Iqra'. Again the Prophet ﷺ answered, 'I cannot read.' A third time the angel embraced him, squeezing harder, then released him and recited:

Read in the Name of your Lord who created — created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous — who taught by the pen — taught man that which he knew not. (Al-Alaq 96:1-5)

Then the angel vanished. The Prophet ﷺ fled the cave, his heart pounding, terrified and shaken. He ran down the mountain, crying out 'Cover me! Cover me!' until he reached home, where Khadijah wrapped him in a blanket and held him close.

In that moment, the world as it was — steeped in idolatry, tribal war, and the oppression of the weak — began to tilt. The final revelation to humanity had started. The age of prophethood was not yet over; it had only just begun.

verse.translation: Read in the Name of your Lord who created — created man from a clinging clot.

milestones.didYouKnow: The first word revealed was 'Iqra' — Read. Not pray, not fast, not give. The Quran opens with a command to seek knowledge.
milestones.takeaway: Before the world can be changed, the heart must first be taught to read.

milestones.title: Khadijah's Belief
milestones.short: The first Muslim, the first supporter of the mission.
milestones.body:
Shaken and trembling, the Prophet ﷺ told Khadijah everything. He feared for himself, feared he was losing his mind, feared the weight of what he had seen. Khadijah — his wife of fifteen years — did not flinch.

She held him, calmed him, and said words that would echo through the ages: 'Allah would never disgrace you. You keep ties of kinship, you carry the burdens of the weak, you give to the poor, you host the guest, you help those struck by calamity.'

She then took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, a learned Christian scholar who had studied the ancient scriptures. When he heard what had happened, his eyes filled with awe. 'This is the same angel who came to Musa (a.s),' he said. 'If only I were alive when your people drive you out — for no man who brings what you bring has ever been left in peace.'

Khadijah became the first Muslim. She believed before anyone else. Waraqah confirmed the truth before his passing shortly after. In one quiet moment, the mission found its first two pillars.
milestones.takeaway: The first believer in any divine mission is often the one closest to home — and their faith keeps it standing through every storm.

milestones.title: Public Preaching Begins
milestones.short: The call at Mount Safa — three years after the secret da'wah.
milestones.body:
For three years, the Prophet ﷺ had called people to Islam quietly — one heart at a time, within his trusted circle. Then the command came to go public.

He climbed Mount Safa, the small hill near the Kaaba, and called out to the tribes of Quraysh by name. One by one, they gathered, curious and uncertain. When they were all seated, he asked them: 'If I told you an army was behind this mountain, ready to attack you, would you believe me?'

They answered without hesitation: 'Yes — we have never known you to lie.'

Then he said: 'Then know that I am a warner to you before a severe punishment. Worship Allah alone. Abandon these idols. If you do not, a punishment will come upon you.'

Silence. Then his uncle Abu Lahab — a man of fierce temper and greater pride — stood up and shouted: 'May you perish! Is this why you gathered us?' The crowd dispersed, mocking and jeering.

But the message had been delivered. From that day forward, Makkah could no longer ignore it. Some mocked. Some walked away. And some — quietly, one by one — began to think.
milestones.takeaway: Truth is not defined by how loudly it is spoken, but by how faithfully it is delivered — even to those who will reject it.

milestones.title: Early Believers
milestones.short: Abu Bakr, Ali, Zayd, Bilal accept Islam.
milestones.body:
Among the first to accept Islam were four people who would come to define its earliest community in Makkah.

Abu Bakr as-Siddiq — a merchant of honour and integrity, the Prophet's ﷺ closest friend even before the revelation. He believed immediately, without hesitation, without question. And through his friendships, others came: Uthman ibn Affan, Talha, Zubayr, Abdurrahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Ali ibn Abi Talib — the Prophet's ﷺ young cousin, raised in his household — believed at the age of ten. He would grow into a warrior, a scholar, and one of the greatest figures in Islamic history.

Zayd ibn Harithah — a freed servant the Prophet ﷺ had adopted as a son — believed at the first call. When his own father came to reclaim him years later, Zayd chose to stay with the Prophet ﷺ over his own family.

And Bilal ibn Rabah — an Abyssinian slave in Makkah — believed quietly, and would pay a heavy price for it. Later, he would become the first muezzin of Islam, his voice calling the Ummah to prayer across the rooftops of Madinah.

These were the first seeds of a community that would one day shake empires.
milestones.takeaway: The first community of any faith is built not from power or wealth, but from a handful of souls willing to stand against everything for what they know is true.

milestones.title: Persecution Begins
milestones.short: The Quraysh tighten their grip on the new Muslims.
milestones.body:
As the number of Muslims grew — quietly, steadily — the Quraysh elders grew uneasy. The message was cutting into their wealth (the idols brought pilgrims and trade), their status (Islam made all believers equal), and their power (it demanded obedience to Allah alone).

At first, they mocked and ridiculed. Then they began to threaten. Then they began to act.

Slaves who had accepted Islam were tortured — Bilal ibn Rabah was dragged across burning sand, stones piled on his chest, until Abu Bakr purchased his freedom. Merchants were boycotted, their trade ruined. Families were torn apart. Some believers were imprisoned. Some were killed.

The Prophet ﷺ himself was protected by his uncle Abu Talib's tribe, so most of the violence fell on the weak, the poor, the enslaved — those who had no one to shield them.

But still they held on. They gathered in secret. They prayed in whispered circles. They did not go back.
milestones.takeaway: The strength of any belief is measured not in the calm, but in the fire — and these first Muslims chose the fire.

milestones.title: First Migration to Abyssinia
milestones.short: A group of Muslims seeks refuge with a Christian king.
milestones.body:
As persecution intensified, the Prophet ﷺ gave a permission that would change history: 'There is a king in Abyssinia — a Christian. He does not wrong anyone. Go to his land, and remain there until Allah makes a way for you.'

Around a hundred Muslims — men, women, and children — quietly slipped out of Makkah, crossed the Red Sea, and arrived at the court of the Negus, King of Abyssinia. It was the first hijrah of Islam.

The Quraysh were furious. They sent two envoys with rich gifts to persuade the king to hand the Muslims back. The envoys argued that these fugitives had abandoned the religion of their fathers for a strange new creed.

The king asked the Muslims what they believed. Their spokesman, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, recited the opening verses of Surah Maryam — the story of Maryam (a.s) and the miraculous birth of Isa (a.s). The king wept. The bishops wept. The Negus declared: 'Truly, this and what Isa brought come from the same source.'

The Muslims were granted safety. It was the first time in Islam's history that a Muslim community lived openly, and the first time a Muslim envoy addressed a foreign king.
milestones.takeaway: The first example of Islam in exile was not conquest — it was a recitation of Maryam, and it brought a Christian king to tears.

milestones.title: Second Migration to Abyssinia
milestones.short: More believers flee; the Negus defends them again.
milestones.body:
The Quraysh's grip tightened further. More Muslims made the journey to Abyssinia — some accounts say over eighty households in total. And the Quraysh sent another delegation, richer than before, determined to bring them back.

They argued that the Muslims had insulted Isa (a.s) and Maryam (a.s) — a lie designed to turn the Christian king against them. The Negus summoned the Muslims again and asked them directly: what do you say about Isa, son of Maryam?

Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered calmly: 'We say of him what our Prophet ﷺ taught — he is the servant of Allah, His Messenger, His Word, and a spirit from Him, sent to the Virgin Maryam.'

The Negus picked up a small stick from the ground and said: 'Isa is not more than this from what you have said.' The bishops murmured, but the king insisted. He refused to hand over a single Muslim. He returned the Quraysh's gifts and sent them home empty-handed.

Islam had found its first safe haven abroad — a Christian kingdom, defending Muslims against the very people who claimed to defend the idols of Makkah.
milestones.takeaway: Allah places safety in the most unexpected places — and sometimes, in the hands of those we never expected to defend us.

milestones.title: Umar and Hamza Accept Islam
milestones.short: Two of the strongest men of Makkah join the believers.
milestones.body:
In the same year, the Muslims received a double blessing that shifted the balance in Makkah: the Islam of Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib and Umar ibn al-Khattab.

Hamza was the Prophet's ﷺ uncle — the strongest, most fearless warrior of the Banu Hashim. He accepted Islam after hearing that Abu Jahl had insulted the Prophet ﷺ. In a fury, Hamza struck Abu Jahl with a bow, declared his Islam, and became a shield for the Muslim community.

Umar ibn al-Khattab was the opposite — the most feared opponent of Islam in Makkah. He had decided to kill the Prophet ﷺ. On his way, he heard that his own sister Fatimah and her husband had accepted Islam. In anger, he beat them both. But when he saw the verses of the Quran they were reading, something changed inside him. He went to the Prophet ﷺ, declared his Islam, and became one of the most fierce and most beloved Muslims in history.

With these two men, the Muslims could finally pray publicly at the Kaaba. The community had teeth.
milestones.takeaway: Allah is not defeated by the fiercest enemies — He simply chooses to turn them into the fiercest defenders.

milestones.title: Boycott of Banu Hashim
milestones.short: Three years in the valley — the Muslims under siege.
milestones.body:
Frustrated by the failure of force, the Quraysh turned to a weapon of collective punishment. They drafted a pact — hung inside the Kaaba — boycotting the Banu Hashim and Banu Muttalib clans entirely.

No trade. No marriage. No shelter. No food. No help. Until the Prophet ﷺ was handed over.

Abu Talib, though not himself a Muslim, led his entire clan into a valley outside Makkah, refusing to surrender his nephew. Around him gathered the believers, the old, the young, the weak — around forty families in total. They lived in that valley for close to three years, in hunger, in cold, in heat, cutting leather to eat, hearing their children cry from emptiness.

Some Quraysh secretly smuggled food in at night — good people who could not bear the cruelty, even if they did not accept Islam.

Then, finally, the pact itself rotted away. Some say a worm ate the words of injustice, leaving only the name of Allah. Others say the boycott simply collapsed under the weight of its own shame. Either way, the Prophet ﷺ and the believers walked out of the valley — thinner, wearier, but unbroken.
milestones.takeaway: Hunger cannot break a soul that has already submitted to Allah — it only teaches it how little it truly needs.

milestones.title: The Year of Sorrow
milestones.short: Khadijah and Abu Talib pass away within months.
milestones.body:
Weakened by three years of hunger, the Prophet ﷺ walked out of the boycott valley into the worst year of his life. In a span of months, he lost the two people who had protected him most.

Abu Talib — his uncle, the man who had raised him as a son, who had shielded him from the Quraysh for over a decade — fell ill and passed away. With his death, the tribal protection that had kept the Prophet ﷺ safe vanished. The Quraysh could now target him openly.

Then, only months later, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid — his wife of twenty-five years, the mother of his children, the first Muslim, the first believer in his message, the one who had wrapped him in a blanket on the day the revelation began — passed away.

The Prophet ﷺ called that year 'the Year of Sorrow.' He had lost both his outer shield and his inner support. For the first time since the revelation, he was truly alone in the world — carrying a mission that grew heavier every day.

Yet he did not waver. He did not complain. He did not turn back. He simply kept going.
milestones.takeaway: When the world takes everything from you, what remains is not your strength — it is your trust in the One who took it.

milestones.title: Journey to Ta'if
milestones.short: Stoned by the mob — he refused to curse the city.
milestones.body:
With Abu Talib and Khadijah gone, the Prophet ﷺ looked beyond Makkah for hearts that would listen. Ta'if — a wealthy city south of Makkah, home to the tribe of Thaqif — seemed hopeful. He travelled there on foot, with only his freed servant Zayd ibn Harithah.

He called the leaders of Ta'if to Islam. They refused, mocked him, and set their street thugs on him. The Prophet ﷺ was chased out of the city, stoned until his sandals filled with blood, driven half a mile into the orchards beyond the walls.

Bleeding and exhausted, he took shelter under a grapevine. The angel Jibril (a.s) came and said: 'Allah has heard what your people said. He has sent the Angel of the Mountains to you — command him to crush them if you wish.' The Prophet ﷺ replied: 'No. I hope that Allah will bring out of their descendants those who will worship Him alone.'

Ta'if later became a Muslim city — not because it was forced, but because it was forgiven.
milestones.takeaway: The strongest answer to cruelty is mercy — and mercy outlives every wound.

milestones.title: Isra and Mi'raj
milestones.short: The night journey — from Makkah to Jerusalem to the heavens.
milestones.body:
It was in the darkest season of the Prophet's ﷺ life — rejected by his own city, wounded by Ta'if, still grieving the loss of Khadijah and Abu Talib — that Allah gave him the greatest gift of his earthly life: the night journey.

In a single night, the Prophet ﷺ was taken by Jibril (a.s) from the Kaaba in Makkah to Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem — this is the Isra. There he led the prophets of old in prayer: Ibrahim (a.s), Musa (a.s), Isa (a.s), and the others — all of them praying behind him, in a silent declaration that he was the final Messenger and Imam of them all.

Then he ascended through the seven heavens — the Mi'raj. He passed through each level, greeting the prophets stationed there: Adam (a.s) in the first heaven, Isa and Yahya (a.s) in the second, Yusuf (a.s) in the third, Idris (a.s) in the fourth, Harun (a.s) in the fifth, Musa (a.s) in the sixth, Ibrahim (a.s) in the seventh. Then he was brought to Sidrat al-Muntaha — the Lote Tree of the Uttermost Boundary — and to the Throne of Allah.

There, the five daily prayers were given to the Ummah. Initially they were fifty. Musa (a.s) advised the Prophet ﷺ to ask for reduction — the Prophet ﷺ returned to his Lord again and again until the burden was lightened to five, though the reward remains as if they were fifty.

He returned to Makkah the same night. When he told the Quraysh, they mocked him. But Abu Bakr — without a moment's hesitation — said: 'If he said it, he spoke the truth.' That is why he is called As-Siddiq: the truthful one.

verse.arabic: سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِ لَيْلًا مِّنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ الْأَقْصَى
verse.translation: Exalted is He who took His Servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa.

milestones.didYouKnow: Musa (a.s) advised the Prophet ﷺ to keep going back to Allah for reduction — the reward for the five prayers is still equivalent to fifty.
milestones.takeaway: When the earth turns against you, Allah opens the heavens — the way out is often upward.

milestones.title: First Pledge of Aqabah
milestones.short: Twelve believers from Yathrib pledge their allegiance.
milestones.body:
During the pilgrimage season, a small group from Yathrib — a city to the north, later to be called Madinah — met the Prophet ﷺ at a place called Aqabah, near Mina. They had heard of him and wanted to know more.

They sat with him, listened to the Quran, and accepted Islam — twelve of them in total. Before returning to Yathrib, they pledged a simple covenant: to worship Allah alone, to not steal, to not commit adultery, to not kill their children, to not slander, and to obey the Prophet ﷺ in what is right.

It was the first pledge of Aqabah — a handshake between the Prophet ﷺ and the first seeds of the Ansar.

He sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr back with them — the first teacher of Islam in Yathrib. Through Mus'ab's quiet work, Islam spread through the city within a year like light through an open window.
milestones.takeaway: A small faithful group is often enough to change a whole city — the seed matters more than the field.

milestones.title: Second Pledge of Aqabah
milestones.short: Seventy-three men and two women pledge to protect the Prophet ﷺ.
milestones.body:
The following year, at the same place, a much larger delegation from Yathrib came — seventy-three men and two women. This time, they pledged something far heavier.

They pledged to protect the Prophet ﷺ as they would protect their own families — with their lives, their wealth, their swords. They pledged to obey him in ease and in hardship, in what they liked and what they disliked. To command good and forbid evil. To speak the truth and fear no one in the way of Allah.

When the pledge was complete, the Prophet ﷺ asked them to choose twelve leaders from among them — naqibs — to represent their tribes. Then he told them: 'You are my representatives among your people. I am the representative of my people among you.'

The Ansar — the Helpers — had declared themselves ready to carry the weight of a mission that was still small and hunted, but would one day shape continents.
milestones.takeaway: Every great movement has an Aqabah — a quiet night when faithful men decide that their lives belong to something bigger.

milestones.title: The Hijrah
milestones.short: The migration to Madinah — the beginning of the Islamic calendar.
milestones.body:
The Quraysh had run out of patience. The Muslims had been persecuted, boycotted, tortured, exiled — and still they were growing. Finally, the chiefs of Makkah reached a decision: it was time to kill the Prophet ﷺ himself. Not publicly, but together — a chosen assassin from each clan, so that no single tribe could be blamed.

Jibril (a.s) came and told the Prophet ﷺ of the plot. The command was given: leave Makkah tonight.

He went to the house of his closest friend, Abu Bakr as-Siddiq. They slipped out of Makkah in the darkness, leaving Ali ibn Abi Talib — still a young man — asleep in the Prophet's ﷺ bed as a decoy. Ali would later return the trusts the Prophet ﷺ held, and then follow to Madinah.

The two fugitives hid in the Cave of Thawr, south of Makkah. The Quraysh searched everywhere; one tracker got so close that Abu Bakr whispered, 'O Messenger of Allah, if one of them looks down at his feet, he will see us.' The Prophet ﷺ replied calmly: 'Do not grieve — indeed, Allah is with us.'

They stayed in the cave three days, then travelled north — a long, hard journey across the desert. Along the way they were nearly captured by Suraqa ibn Malik, a rider hunting for the Quraysh's reward. The Prophet ﷺ prayed for him, and Suraqa's horse sank into the sand. Twice more he tried, and twice more his horse failed. Finally, he asked for safety, promised to help, and let them go. Years later, Suraqa came to the Prophet ﷺ as a Muslim.

After roughly two weeks of travel, the Prophet ﷺ arrived at the oasis of Yathrib. He was greeted by the Ansar with joy that has few parallels in history. The city would soon be known by a new name: Madinat an-Nabi — the City of the Prophet. Al-Madinah.

That year — 622 CE — became year one of the Islamic calendar. Not the year of his birth. Not the year of the first revelation. The year of the Hijrah — the year the Ummah found a home.

verse.translation: If you do not aid him — Allah has already aided him.

milestones.didYouKnow: The Islamic calendar does not start from the Prophet's ﷺ birth or the first revelation — it starts from the Hijrah, because that is when the Ummah became a community.
milestones.takeaway: Sometimes the journey away from home is the journey toward home — Allah moves His servants when the time for the next chapter has come.

milestones.title: Masjid an-Nabawi Built
milestones.short: The first mosque of Madinah rises from the sand.
milestones.body:
The Prophet's ﷺ camel, Qaswa, knelt on a piece of land in Madinah — and he said: 'This, if Allah wills, is our resting place.' The land belonged to two orphan boys, who offered it as a gift. The Prophet ﷺ insisted on paying for it, then set to work.

He carried mud bricks with his own hands. Abu Bakr carried bricks. Umar carried bricks. Uthman carried bricks. Muhajirun and Ansar worked side by side — nobles and freed slaves, rich and poor, all building the first home of Islam in Madinah.

The mosque was simple: palm trunks as pillars, palm fronds as roof, a floor of sand and stone. Around it, small apartments were built for the Prophet's ﷺ family. The Ahl as-Suffah — the poorest of the believers — were housed under a shaded section; they would become the first students of the Islamic school.

From this simple structure, the Prophet ﷺ would teach, judge, pray, and command. It was not a palace. It was not a fortress. It was a place of prayer and a place of peace — and the world would look at it for the rest of history.
milestones.takeaway: The greatest institutions in history have been built from the humblest materials — what matters is what is grown inside them.

milestones.title: The Constitution of Madinah
milestones.short: A written charter uniting Muslims, Jews, and tribes under one city.
milestones.body:
Madinah was not a single city — it was a patchwork of tribes: the Aws, the Khazraj, several Jewish tribes, and now the Muhajirun from Makkah. Old blood feuds ran deep. If the Prophet ﷺ was to build a community, he first needed a peace.

He drafted a document — the Constitution of Madinah — one of the earliest written constitutions in human history. It declared that all the tribes of Madinah, Muslim and Jewish, formed a single Ummah — one community — with each group keeping its own religion, its own laws, and its own customs.

It set out mutual defence: if Madinah was attacked, all would defend it together. It set out justice: disputes would be settled by the Prophet ﷺ. It set out mercy: no one would be wronged because of his faith.

It was not a Muslim state ruling over non-Muslims. It was a shared city with a shared promise — and for a while, it worked.
milestones.takeaway: True leadership does not impose unity — it builds a home where different people can live as one.

milestones.title: Change of Qibla
milestones.short: From Jerusalem to the Kaaba — the Ummah finds its own direction.
milestones.body:
Since the beginning of Islam, the Muslims had prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis — the Sacred House in Jerusalem — the qibla of the earlier prophets. But the Prophet ﷺ longed for a different direction. He would stand in prayer, eyes lifted to the sky, silently asking Allah to turn him toward the Kaaba of Ibrahim (a.s) — the house his ancestor had built.

Then one day, mid-prayer in Madinah, the revelation came. The Prophet ﷺ turned where he stood, and the entire congregation turned with him — from north to south, from Jerusalem to Makkah.

The moment was more than a change of direction. It was a declaration of independence. Islam was not a branch of Judaism or Christianity. It was its own Ummah, with its own qibla, its own prophet, its own book. The Kaaba — the first house of worship built for humanity — was now the centre of the Muslim world.
milestones.takeaway: The direction you face shapes the person you become — Islam gives its people their own compass.

milestones.title: Battle of Badr
milestones.short: 313 believers against 1,000 Quraysh — the Day of Distinction.
milestones.body:
In Ramadan of the second year after the Hijrah, the Muslims received news that a large Quraysh caravan — loaded with goods seized from the Muhajirun when they fled Makkah — was returning from Syria under the guard of Abu Sufyan. The Prophet ﷺ set out with 313 men to intercept it. It was not a battle he sought; it was an act of reclaiming stolen property.

But Abu Sufyan learned of the plan, sent word to Makkah, and the entire city mobilised. Nearly 1,000 Quraysh warriors — the pride of Arabia, armed and mounted — marched north to defend the caravan and crush the Muslims for good.

The two armies met at the wells of Badr. The Muslims had 313 men, 2 horses, and 70 camels. They were outnumbered three to one. Some of them had no weapons. Many of them were freed slaves, young men, and elderly believers.

The night before, the Prophet ﷺ spent hours in prayer, weeping, his hands raised to the sky: 'O Allah, if this small band is destroyed, there will be no one left on earth to worship You.'

At dawn, the battle began. The Prophet ﷺ threw a handful of dust toward the enemy and said: 'May their faces be deformed.' Then the fighting started — and within hours, it was over. The Quraysh were routed. Their greatest warriors were killed or captured. Seventy of their men lay dead; the Muslims lost fourteen.

The Quran would later call that day Yawm al-Furqan — the Day of Distinction — the moment when truth and falsehood were separated forever.

verse.arabic: وَلَقَدْ نَصَرَكُمُ اللَّهُ بِبَدْرٍ وَأَنتُمْ أَذِلَّةٌ
verse.translation: And Allah had certainly helped you at Badr when you were weak.

milestones.didYouKnow: The angel Jibril (a.s) descended with a thousand angels on that day — Badr is the only battle in Islamic history confirmed in the Quran as having divine reinforcements.
milestones.takeaway: Victory is not measured by numbers — it is granted to whoever trusts Allah most completely.

milestones.title: Battle of Uhud
milestones.short: The archers' error — the Prophet ﷺ is wounded.
milestones.body:
The Quraysh did not accept Badr. In the following year, they returned with 3,000 warriors — three times the size of the Muslim force — with the wealth of their caravan paying for horses, armour, and camels. They marched on Madinah to avenge their dead.

The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions. Many of the young men wanted to meet the enemy in open battle outside the city; the elders preferred to defend from within. The Prophet ﷺ agreed to go out. He wore two coats of armour, one over the other.

He placed fifty archers on a small hill — Mount ar-Rumah — with one clear command: 'Stay here. Do not leave your post, no matter what you see. If we are winning, do not come help us. If we are losing, do not come rescue us.'

The battle began well. The Muslims held their lines, and the Quraysh began to waver. Then the archers saw the enemy starting to retreat — and they saw their comrades collecting the spoils. They decided to join the spoils, leaving their post. Their commander warned them: 'The Prophet ﷺ ordered us to stay!' But most of them descended the hill.

Khalid ibn al-Walid — then still a Quraysh commander — saw the opening. He led his cavalry around the hill, struck the Muslims from behind, and the Muslim lines collapsed into chaos. The Prophet ﷺ was wounded — his face cut, his tooth chipped. Rumours spread that he had been killed; the Muslims broke apart, some fleeing back toward Madinah, others fighting to the death around the Prophet ﷺ.

Among the martyrs that day was Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib — the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, the lion of Quraysh — killed by a spear thrown by Wahshi, a slave acting for his master. When the Prophet ﷺ found his body, he wept.

Around seventy Muslims were killed. The Quraysh, though victorious on the field, did not push on to Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ buried his companions, comforted the wounded, and prepared his community to learn — hard — from its mistake.

Uhud taught the Muslims a lesson no victory could have: obedience to the Prophet ﷺ is not optional, and discipline is the price of Allah's help.

verse.arabic: وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ إِذْ تَحُسُّونَهُم بِإِذْنِهِ
verse.translation: And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission.

milestones.didYouKnow: Uhud taught a lesson that has echoed through Islamic history: the Muslim Ummah loses not because the enemy is stronger, but when it disobeys the guidance it has been given.
milestones.takeaway: Victory is not the sign of Allah's pleasure, nor defeat of His anger — the sign is whether you stayed faithful to the command.

milestones.title: Battle of the Trench
milestones.short: The city is besieged; Allah sends a storm.
milestones.body:
After Uhud, the Quraysh wanted one final strike — something that would end the Muslims once and for all. They sent envoys across Arabia, gathering every tribe, every clan, every mercenary they could find. They even recruited the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir, expelled from Madinah earlier, who joined the war effort with money and men.

The result: an army of nearly 10,000. Ten thousand warriors, mounted and armed, marching on a city of a few thousand defenders. The largest army Madinah had ever faced.

The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions. Salman al-Farsi — a Persian Muslim, learned in the military tactics of his homeland — proposed something Arabia had never seen: dig a trench. A wide, deep trench around the exposed northern flank of Madinah, where an army of that size would have to cross. The Prophet ﷺ loved the idea.

The Muslims dug for days. Hundreds of them, in the cold of a Madinan winter, cutting into hard earth, some of them without proper food or clothing. The Prophet ﷺ dug alongside them, singing poems of encouragement, his hands blistered like everyone else's.

When the enemy arrived, they found the trench — and they were stunned. Their horses could not cross. Their archers could not dislodge the Muslims. For nearly a month, the two armies faced off across the ditch. Skirmishes. Arrows. Taunts. Nothing decisive.

Then the Prophet ﷺ prayed — and the prayer was answered. A violent storm rose one night. Winds tore their tents, uprooted their fires, scattered their horses. The Qur'an says: Allah sent a wind and soldiers you could not see. By morning, the confederates were gone. The siege collapsed. The city survived.

The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Now we will attack them. They will not attack us.' From that day, the Quraysh never again marched on Madinah.

verse.arabic: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذْ جَاءَتْكُمْ جُنُودٌ فَأَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ رِيحًا
verse.translation: O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you when armies came to you and We sent upon them a wind.

milestones.didYouKnow: The trench — Salman al-Farsi's idea — was the first use of defensive trench warfare in Arabian history. The Muslims learned from the world and let Allah do the rest.
milestones.takeaway: When you exhaust every means available, Allah will send soldiers you cannot see — but only after you have done your part.

milestones.title: Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
milestones.short: A seeming defeat — the beginning of the greatest victory.
milestones.body:
Six years after the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ led 1,400 Muslims toward Makkah — not to fight, but to perform Umrah. He had made peace the goal. Around the neck of his camel hung garlands, clearly showing they were pilgrims, not warriors.

But the Quraysh refused. They would not allow the Muslims to enter Makkah, not even for pilgrimage. They sent envoys. They argued. They refused every offer. The Prophet ﷺ eventually stopped at a place called Hudaybiyyah, just outside the sanctuary.

Then something unusual happened: the Muslims pledged their lives to the Prophet ﷺ under a tree — a pledge of loyalty, of obedience, of willingness to fight if needed. The Quran would later call it Bay'at ar-Ridwan — the Pledge of Pleasure.

And then — negotiations reopened. The Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn Amr. The two sides agreed to a truce, ten years of peace. But the terms were astonishingly hard on the Muslims:

— The Muslims would not perform Umrah this year — they would go home, and return next year.
— Any Makkan who fled to Madinah without his guardian's permission would be returned to the Quraysh.
— But any Muslim who fled to Makkah would not be returned.
— All tribes were free to ally with either side.

The Muslims were shocked. Umar ibn al-Khattab could not bear it. 'Are we not on the truth, and they on falsehood?' he asked. The Prophet ﷺ stayed calm: 'I am the servant of Allah. He will not abandon me.'

They went home without completing Umrah. Many were close to despair.

But within two years, Surah al-Fath was revealed — the Chapter of Victory — declaring that Allah had given the Muslims a clear victory. Because of the peace, the two sides could finally speak without swords. Islam spread through Arabia faster than it ever had. Within a few years, more people entered Islam than had entered it in the previous nineteen.

Hudaybiyyah proved that not every victory comes with a sword. Sometimes, the greatest triumph is the quiet one.

verse.translation: Indeed, We have given you a clear victory.

milestones.didYouKnow: After Hudaybiyyah, more people entered Islam in two years than in the previous nineteen — the truce gave the message of Islam its greatest reach.
milestones.takeaway: The greatest victories are sometimes disguised as defeats — only patience reveals them.

milestones.title: Letters to the Kings
milestones.short: The Prophet ﷺ writes to Heraclius, Khosrow, and the Muqawqis.
milestones.body:
After Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ did something no Arab leader had ever done: he sent letters — formal invitations to Islam — to the great rulers of the world. He sent them to Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium. To Khosrow, King of Persia. To the Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt. To the Negus of Abyssinia. To the kings of Yemen, Bahrain, and other lands.

The letters were short and dignified. Each began with Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Raheem. Each called the ruler to Islam, without threats, without arrogance. They said, in essence: I am the Messenger of Allah. Accept Islam and you will be safe. If you refuse, you bear the sin of your people.

The responses varied. The Negus accepted Islam in private, and remained a Christian king to his people. The Muqawqis sent gifts and a polite refusal. Heraclius is said to have been moved, even convinced, but did not embrace Islam publicly, fearing the loss of his throne. Khosrow, King of Persia — proud and arrogant — tore the letter in pieces. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'May Allah tear his kingdom as he tore my letter.' Within a few years, the Persian empire fell.

The letters were not a conquest. They were an announcement: the message of Islam was not for a tribe, or a region, or an age. It was for the world.
milestones.takeaway: The mission of Islam was never tribal — it was global — and the Prophet ﷺ announced this with ink and words before he ever did with armies.

milestones.title: Battle of Mu'tah
milestones.short: First encounter with the Romans — three commanders fall.
milestones.body:
The Prophet ﷺ sent an envoy, al-Harith ibn Umayr, with a letter to the ruler of Busra, in Byzantine territory. The envoy was stopped at a place called Mu'tah, and killed — a violation of every law of diplomacy among the Arabs.

The Prophet ﷺ sent 3,000 Muslims to respond. He appointed Zayd ibn Harithah as commander, then said: 'If Zayd falls, then Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. If Ja'far falls, then Abdullah ibn Rawahah. If he falls, then let the Muslims choose.'

When the Muslims reached Mu'tah, they found not the small garrison they expected but the full Byzantine army — reinforced by Arab tribes — numbering in the hundreds of thousands. Still, they fought. Zayd ibn Harithah was killed. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib was killed. Abdullah ibn Rawahah was killed. Three commanders fell in succession.

The Muslims chose Khalid ibn al-Walid — recently converted, and about to become the most famous general in Islamic history. Khalid reorganised the troops, withdrew them in good order, and saved the Muslim army.

There was no victory at Mu'tah. But there was also no rout. And the Prophet ﷺ said: 'They are all in Paradise' — of Zayd, Ja'far, and Abdullah. It was the first time the Muslims faced the Romans — and they had held their ground.
milestones.takeaway: Some battles are not fought to be won, but to be fought well — and Allah honours the ones who stood.

milestones.title: Expedition to Khaybar
milestones.short: The last stronghold of the hostile tribes in Arabia is opened.
milestones.body:
Khaybar was a fortress town north of Madinah — wealthy, well-defended, and home to the last of the tribes who had helped besiege the Muslims during the Battle of the Trench. After Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ turned his attention to Khaybar.

The Muslims marched with 1,600 men. The fortresses of Khaybar were formidable — built into rocky hills, layered in defence, protected by skilled archers. For days, the Muslims could not break through.

Then the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love.' The companions spent the night wondering who it would be. In the morning, he called Ali ibn Abi Talib — who was recovering from an eye infection — and applied his saliva to Ali's eyes. The infection vanished. He gave Ali the banner and said: 'Advance gently. Call them to Islam first. If even one person is guided through you, it is better for you than a herd of red camels.'

Ali led the assault. The fortresses fell one by one. The Muslims were victorious, and the lands and properties of Khaybar were divided fairly — the Jews were allowed to remain as farmers, working the land in partnership with the Muslims.

Khaybar was not just a military victory. It was the moment the Muslims became a regional power in Arabia — and the moment Ali ibn Abi Talib emerged as a warrior of legend.
milestones.takeaway: The banner of victory is given not to the strongest, but to the most beloved of Allah — strength of heart outweighs strength of arm.

milestones.title: Conquest of Makkah
milestones.short: Head bowed low on his camel — a general amnesty for his enemies.
milestones.body:
Two years after Hudaybiyyah, the Quraysh violated the treaty — their allies attacked a tribe allied with the Muslims, and the Quraysh themselves helped with weapons. The truce was broken. The Prophet ﷺ now had the right to march on Makkah.

He did not tell anyone where he was going. Ten thousand Muslims — the largest army Islam had ever assembled — marched quietly toward Makkah, arriving at the outskirts in the month of Ramadan, 630 CE. The Quraysh were caught completely unprepared. Abu Sufyan, the old enemy, came out to negotiate. He accepted Islam. His wife Hind — the woman who had torn out Hamza's liver at Uhud — also accepted Islam. The leadership of Quraysh had fallen.

The Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah not in triumph, but in humility. He rode on his camel with his head bowed so low that his beard nearly touched the saddle — such was his fear of Allah on the day of his greatest victory. He recited Surah al-Fath as he entered. No mass executions. No revenge. No looting.

He went straight to the Kaaba. Around it stood 360 idols, placed by the Quraysh over centuries. He stood before each one, reciting: 'Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is bound to vanish.' And he struck each one down with his staff. The Kaaba was cleansed.

Then he called the people of Makkah together — the very people who had tortured him, exiled him, killed his companions, driven him out of his own city. He asked them: 'What do you think I will do with you?' They answered: 'Good — you are a noble brother, son of a noble brother.'

The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Go. You are free.'

General amnesty. Thousands embraced Islam that day. Not because they were forced, but because they were forgiven.

Makkah — the city that had tried to kill him — was now the spiritual heart of Islam.

verse.arabic: وَقُلْ جَاءَ الْحَقُّ وَزَهَقَ الْبَاطِلُ ۚ إِنَّ الْبَاطِلَ كَانَ زَهُوقًا
verse.translation: And say: Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is bound to vanish.

milestones.didYouKnow: The Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah with his head bowed so low on his camel that his beard nearly touched the saddle — he was more humble on his day of greatest victory than at any other time in his life.
milestones.takeaway: The greatest leaders conquer not with vengeance but with mercy — they win the hearts of those they defeat.

milestones.title: Battle of Hunayn
milestones.short: The first test after Makkah — a new lesson in trust.
milestones.body:
The conquest of Makkah had barely settled when news came that two powerful tribes — Hawazin and Thaqif — were gathering forces to attack. The Prophet ﷺ marched out with 12,000 warriors — the largest army he had ever led, fresh from victory.

But at the valley of Hunayn, the Muslims walked into an ambush. The Hawazin had hidden their best archers in the hills around the narrow valley. When the Muslims marched in, arrows rained down from every side. Many fled. For a moment, the army seemed on the brink of collapse.

The Prophet ﷺ stayed. He called out: 'I am the Prophet — this is no lie! I am the son of Abdul-Muttalib!' His uncle Abbas called out to the Muhajirun and the Ansar, rallying them back. The believers regrouped, held their ground, and turned the ambush into a decisive victory. The Hawazin were routed. Their families and flocks were taken as spoils.

Then the delegation of Hawazin came, and among them a woman who had nursed the Prophet ﷺ as an infant — Halimah's daughter, his foster sister, al-Shayma. He spread out his cloak for her, and offered her gifts. When the tribe asked him to return their families and wealth, he consulted the Muslims, and most of them gave up their shares. The captives were freed.

It was a lesson: victory does not come from numbers, but from hearts that stay standing when the tide turns.
milestones.takeaway: Numbers give confidence, but only steadfast hearts give victory — Hunayn taught this harder than any battle before.

milestones.title: Year of Delegations
milestones.short: Tribes across Arabia send envoys to accept Islam.
milestones.body:
After Makkah was opened and Hunayn was won, a new phenomenon appeared in Arabia: tribes began sending delegations to Madinah to accept Islam. Not one by one, but in waves.

The Prophet ﷺ received them all with dignity and generosity. He taught them the basics of the religion, appointed teachers and imams among them, and sent them home with gifts and letters. He never demanded tribute, never humiliated anyone, never forced a tribe to surrender its pride.

The tribal leaders expected him to behave like a king; he behaved like a shepherd. They expected him to sit on a throne; he sat on the sand. They expected arrogance from a victor; they found humility.

That was the year the Arabs called the Year of Delegations — the year Islam became the religion of Arabia.
milestones.takeaway: When a cause reaches a certain scale, it no longer needs to fight — it simply needs to stay true to itself.

milestones.title: Expedition to Tabuk
milestones.short: The last major expedition — marched to the doorstep of Rome.
milestones.body:
Intelligence reached Madinah that the Byzantine Emperor had gathered an enormous force at Tabuk, in the far north of Arabia, to crush the Muslims once and for all. The Prophet ﷺ called for the largest expedition he had ever prepared. It was the height of summer. The distance was long. The harvest was ripe. The people were tired.

This was the moment Uthman ibn Affan's wealth became legendary. He funded a third of the army's expenses from his own pocket. Abu Bakr gave everything he owned. Umar gave half. The Muslims gave what they could. Thirty thousand men — the largest Muslim army yet — marched north to Tabuk.

They reached Tabuk, at the edge of Byzantine territory. But there was no enemy. The Rum had withdrawn. The Prophet ﷺ stayed for a few days, made treaties with the local Christian tribes, and returned to Madinah.

No battle was fought. But Tabuk proved something crucial: the Muslims could now march wherever they wished, and their enemies were afraid of them. Islam had become a regional power — not through conquest, but through presence.
milestones.takeaway: Sometimes the purpose of a march is not the battle at the end — it is what the marching itself proves.

milestones.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage
milestones.short: The only Hajj after the Hijrah — and the final message to all humanity.
milestones.body:
In the tenth year after the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ made the announcement many had been waiting for: he would perform Hajj. Word spread across Arabia. By the time he set out from Madinah, over 100,000 Muslims had joined him — a vast crowd, all wearing the same two simple white cloths, all answering the Talbiyah together.

They travelled to Makkah, performed Tawaf, Sa'i, and the rites of Hajj. On the ninth day — the Day of Arafah — the Prophet ﷺ stood on the plain of Arafah before more than 100,000 companions.

And then he delivered the greatest sermon ever delivered from a mountain. Not a military address. Not a declaration of victory. A farewell.

He said: 'O people, listen to my words. I do not know whether I will ever meet you again in this place after this year. Your lives and your property are sacred — as sacred as this day, this month, this city. Return the trusts to their owners. Do not harm one another. Know that every Muslim is a brother to every Muslim. You are all equal — no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, no white to a black, except by piety and good deeds.'

He addressed the rights of women: 'Fear Allah concerning women. You have rights over them, and they have rights over you.'

He told them: 'I am leaving among you something that if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah.'

Then he asked them: 'Have I conveyed the message?' And the vast crowd answered with one voice: 'Yes.' And he said: 'O Allah, bear witness.'

That day, the verse descended: 'This day I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favour upon you, and chosen for you Islam as your religion.'

It was the completion of the message. Twenty-three years of revelation, of struggle, of patience, of building — all of it had reached its completion on that mountain, in that moment, before that crowd.

He returned to Madinah. The mission was finished.

verse.arabic: الْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِي وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ الْإِسْلَامَ دِينًا
verse.translation: This day I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favour upon you, and chosen for you Islam as your religion.

milestones.didYouKnow: The Farewell Sermon was delivered to over 100,000 Muslims — one of the earliest recorded declarations of universal human rights, centuries before the Magna Carta.
milestones.takeaway: The message was complete the day the Prophet ﷺ asked the Ummah 'Have I conveyed it?' — and the Ummah is responsible for answering yes by living it.

milestones.title: The Passing of the Prophet ﷺ
milestones.short: In the room of Aishah (RA), aged 63.
milestones.body:
Two months after the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ began to feel the weight of the end. He had begun to tire more easily. He would pray sitting down. He told his companions, subtly, that he felt this would be the end.

One day, he asked his companions: 'If you were given the choice between the treasures of the world and the meeting with your Lord, what would you choose?' Abu Bakr understood immediately and wept. He knew the Prophet ﷺ was telling them something.

In his final days, he asked for the doors of the mosque to be closed except the door of Abu Bakr. Then he asked Aishah (RA) for permission to spend his last days in her room — she, the one he loved most after Khadijah.

On the morning of his final day, he woke and looked toward the mosque. The Muslims were praying. He smiled. Then he raised his hand and gestured: as-salah, as-salah — the prayer, the prayer. It was his last instruction to his Ummah: prayer.

Then he grew silent. Aishah (RA) held his head against her chest. She heard him whisper, one last time: 'O Allah, forgive me and have mercy on me, and join me to the Most High Companion.' And then he passed away — his head resting against Aishah's chest, in her room, on the mat beside her bed. It was the year 632 CE. He was 63 years old.

Umar ibn al-Khattab refused to believe it. He stood among the people, sword in hand, threatening to strike anyone who said the Prophet ﷺ had died. Then Abu Bakr entered, uncovered the Prophet's ﷺ face, kissed his forehead, and wept: 'May my father and mother be sacrificed for you, O Messenger of Allah. You were beautiful in life, and you are beautiful in death.'

Then he went outside and spoke to the people: 'O people, whoever worshipped Muhammad — Muhammad is dead. But whoever worships Allah — Allah is alive and never dies.'

And he recited the verse: 'Muhammad is no more than a Messenger, and Messengers have passed before him. Will you, if he dies or is killed, turn back on your heels?'

The Ummah's grief was beyond words. But the Ummah's faith was not in a man. It was in Allah.

verse.arabic: وَمَا مُحَمَّدٌ إِلَّا رَسُولٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ الرُّسُلُ
verse.translation: Muhammad is no more than a Messenger, and Messengers have passed before him.

milestones.didYouKnow: The Prophet ﷺ asked to spend his last days in Aishah's room, and asked for her door to the mosque to remain open. He passed away with his head resting against her chest — a final, tender moment between two souls who had shared the greatest story ever told.
milestones.takeaway: The Prophet ﷺ was human — he loved, he grieved, he suffered, he died. But the message he carried was divine, and it did not die with him.

milestones.title: Burial in Aishah's Chamber
milestones.short: He was buried where he passed — in the room of the one he loved.
milestones.body:
After his passing, the companions disagreed on where to bury the Prophet ﷺ — Makkah, Madinah's main mosque, or somewhere else. Abu Bakr reminded them of what the Prophet ﷺ had said: 'Every prophet is buried where he dies.' So he was buried in Aishah's chamber, beneath the very spot where his soul had left this world.

Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Talha ibn Ubaydullah (RA) washed his body. He was wrapped in three white cloths. Jibril (a.s) — say the narrations — attended the washing in the form of a companion no one recognised. The companions prayed over him in small groups, without an imam, one group after another, for the entire day and night.

He was buried on the night of Wednesday, in the chamber of Aishah (RA). His grave was simple — a small stone was placed to mark the spot, and nothing more.

The house in which he died, and the chamber in which he was buried, were later absorbed into the Masjid an-Nabawi. Today, beneath the green dome of the Prophet's ﷺ Mosque in Madinah, lies the Messenger of Allah — waiting, as he promised, to rise again on the Day of Judgement.
milestones.takeaway: Every prophet returns to the earth — but the message lives on as long as there are hearts to carry it.
